content.page_title: 14.1.2 New heart failure presenting during pregnancy; 14.2 Cardiomyopathies

sections.heading: New heart failure presenting during pregnancy
key_points: Increased circulatory volume and cardiac output in pregnancy can unmask pre-existing but undiagnosed causes of heart failure such as cardiomyopathies (CMPs) and valvular disease.
Symptoms more likely in second trimester when cardiac output demand is highest; severe emotional stress in pregnancy/delivery can cause Takotsubo syndrome.

Assessment: detailed cardiac assessment with echocardiography, natriuretic peptide (NP) levels, foetal ultrasound and foetal monitoring recommended; consider non-contrast CMR if diagnostic uncertainty.

sections.heading: Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM)
definition_and_timing: PPCM presents as heart failure secondary to left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction, usually with LVEF <45%, occurring towards the end of pregnancy (third trimester) or in months following delivery without other identifiable cause.
Majority of PPCM cases are diagnosed post-partum.
epidemiology: Prevalence reported as approximately 1:100 in Nigeria, 1:1000 in South Africa, and 1:1500 in Germany.
Prospective cohort studies report 6-month mortality ranging from 2.0% in Germany to 12.6% in a 206-patient PPCM cohort from South Africa.
clinical_presentation_and_prognosis: Frequently presents with acute heart failure; may present with ventricular arrhythmias and/or cardiac arrest.
Adverse features: LVEF <30%, marked LV dilatation, LV end-diastolic diameter >6.0 cm, and right ventricular involvement.
Cardiac recovery may occur in first 3–6 months but can be delayed up to 2 years; recovery rates vary regionally (reported 75% to <50%).
management: Milder cases: oral diuretics, beta-blockers, hydralazine, and oral nitrates.
Pregnant women with signs of acute HF require urgent hospital admission.

Severe PPCM with cardiogenic shock: consider transfer to advanced HF centre for ECMO, LVAD and/or cardiac transplantation; consider urgent delivery by caesarean section with MCS immediately available.
Adrenergic agents (dobutamine, adrenaline) may be detrimental; when haemodynamically unstable consider levosimendan or mechanical circulatory support (MCS).
LVAD implantation as bridge-to-transplant (BTT) or bridge-to-recovery (BTR) may be considered in refractory cardiogenic shock.
bromocriptine: Bromocriptine proposed to reduce production of a cleaved 16 kDa prolactin fragment that may contribute to PPCM pathophysiology.

Randomized trial tested bromocriptine in 63 patients comparing long-term (8 weeks) vs short-term (1 week) treatment; associated with recovery of LV function and no difference between regimens in that trial.
Considerations: bromocriptine may increase risk of deep venous thrombosis and causes cessation of lactation; if started, prophylactic (or therapeutic) anticoagulation should accompany treatment.

sections.heading: 14.2 Cardiomyopathies
key_points: Cardiomyopathies (CMPs) can be inherited (genetic/familial) and/or acquired. They are a heterogeneous group of diseases and major causes of heart failure.
CMPs can be accelerated by disease modifiers.
